item.title: Big names back forum | FABC marks 40 years of Fiji-Australia business ties
item.description: The 2026 Fiji-Australia Business Council (FABC) and Australia-Fiji Business Council (AFBC) Joint Business Forum has today announced a powerhouse line-up of strategic partners for the upcoming landmark event at Suva’s Grand Pacific Hotel from August 27–29. This year’s forum holds special significance as it coincides with the 40th Ruby Anniversary of the Fiji-Australia Business Council (FABC).
item.content:encoded:
The 2026 Fiji-Australia Business Council (FABC) and Australia-Fiji Business Council (AFBC) Joint Business Forum has today announced a powerhouse line-up of strategic partners for the upcoming landmark event at Suva’s Grand Pacific Hotel from August 27–29.

This year’s forum holds special significance as it coincides with the 40th Ruby Anniversary of the Fiji-Australia Business Council (FABC).

Since its inception, the FABC has been at the forefront of fostering friendship, goodwill, and economic cooperation between the two nations. Celebrating four decades of impact, the Council continues to provide the premier platform for high-level dialogue and regional collaboration.

Under the overarching theme ‘Strategy for a shifting landscape’, the forum is being propelled by the region’s leaders in finance, telecommunications, logistics, and commercial services.

Westpac Fiji, a Gold sponsor and one of the Pacific’s longest-standing financial institutions, leads the charge in fostering economic resilience.

“Westpac Fiji is proud to support the 2026 Joint Business Forum,” the bank stated.

“As a long-term partner in Fiji’s economic development, we remain committed to connecting people, supporting businesses, and fostering the partnerships that drive sustainable growth and opportunity across our region.”

The forum’s digital and technology landscape is anchored by Digicel Pacific.

As part of the Telstra family, Digicel’s involvement highlights its role as an essential enabler of cross-border commerce, focusing on 5G rollout, secure cloud architecture, and digital wallet ecosystems like MyCash to help businesses stay resilient.

Critical to navigating the shifting landscape is the reliability of trade routes.

Swire Shipping, with more than 80 years of service in the South Pacific, joins the forum to highlight the vital role of logistics.

“Our objective is to highlight the vital role shipping plays in enabling economic growth and resilient supply chains,” Swire Shipping noted.

“Our fortnightly fixed-day window service between Australia and Fiji provides businesses with the reliability needed to grow trade across the region.”

Local commercial excellence is represented by Vision Commercial, focusing on innovation and sustainable commercial practices.

“Vision Commercial is honoured to support this important platform,” said Rajneel Kishor, senior commercial manager.

“We believe that collaboration, innovation, and investment in our business community are key drivers of sustainable economic growth.”

Rounding out the high-level support is AquaSafe, celebrating its 30th year of operation and its role as a major sponsor of the Fijian Drua.

AquaSafe noted that the councils fulfil a “critical role in facilitating trade and fostering strong ties between governments”.

FABC secretariat, Lisa Apted, emphasised that the calibre of these partnerships and the Council’s 40-year legacy reflected the high stakes of the current regional environment.

“This 40th Ruby Anniversary is a significant milestone for FABC, marking four decades of dedicated service to the Fiji-Australia business relationship,” Ms Apted stated.

“The alignment of our partners with this year’s theme ensures that the forum is not just a celebration of our history, but a launchpad for the next chapter of regional commercial execution. Don’t just adapt to the future of Pacific business – be in the room where it’s being built.”

With delegate numbers approaching capacity, registrations will officially close in the coming week.

Business leaders, exporters, and investors are urged to complete their bookings immediately via the official FABC website to guarantee participation in this anniversary event.

item.title: Preventing diabetic retinopathy: Protecting your vision before it’s too late
item.description: DIABETES is becoming an increasing health concern in Fiji, and one of its most serious complications is diabetic retinopathy — a condition that can permanently damage the eyes and lead to vision loss. item.content:encoded:
DIABETES is becoming an increasing health concern in Fiji, and one of its most serious complications is diabetic retinopathy — a condition that can permanently damage the eyes and lead to vision loss. The good news is that diabetic eye disease can often be prevented, detected early, and treated eff ectively if people take the right steps. Diabetic retinopathy occurs when prolonged high blood sugar damages the tiny blood vessels supplying the retina, the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye. In the early stages, a person may have no symptoms at all. This is why wait ing until vision becomes blurry is not a safe approach.

The most important step in preventing diabetic retinopathy is maintaining good blood glucose control. Persistently high blood sugar damages retinal blood vessels and increases the risk of bleeding, swelling and abnormal blood-vessel growth inside the eye. People with diabetes should regularly monitor their blood glucose and follow the treatment plan recommended by their doctor. A healthy diet, regular physical activity, maintaining a healthy weight and taking prescribed medication consistently can significantly reduce the risk of diabetic complications.

Diabetes does not affect the eyes alone. High blood pressure and abnormal cholesterol levels can further damage the retinal blood vessels. People with diabetes should therefore have their blood pressure and cholesterol checked regularly. Controlling these conditions, together with blood sugar, provides better protection against diabetic eye disease.

One of the most important messages for every person with diabetes is: do not wait for symptoms before having your eyes examined. Diabetic retinopathy can develop without pain or noticeable changes in vision. A comprehensive eye examination can identify retinal changes before significant vision is lost. Depending on the individual’s condition, an eye-care professional may examine the retina using specialised instruments and may recommend retinal photography, optical coherence tomography (OCT), or other tests. The frequency of examinations depends on the type of diabetes, duration of diabetes, blood sugar control and whether retinal disease is already present.

People with diabetes should seek an eye examination promptly if they experience sudden or gradual changes in vision, new floaters, flashes of light, dark spots, distorted vision or a sudden loss of sight. These symptoms can indicate bleeding, retinal swelling or other complications that require urgent assessment.

Protecting your eyes starts with protecting your overall health. Regular physical activity, eating a balanced diet with plenty of vegetables and fibre, avoiding smoking and limiting unhealthy foods can help improve diabetes control and reduce the risk of complications. It is also important to take diabetes medication as prescribed and attend regular medical appointments.

The encouraging message is that diabetic retinopathy does not have to mean blindness. Modern treatments, including injections into the eye, laser treatment and surgery when necessary, can help preserve or improve vision in many patients. However, treatment is much more effective when the condition is detected early. For Fiji, improving awareness of diabetic eye disease is especially important. People living with diabetes should make regular eye examinations part of their diabetes care, just as they monitor their blood sugar, blood pressure and other aspects of their health. Your eyes may feel perfectly normal while diabetes is silently damaging them. Do not wait until you lose vision. Control your diabetes, check your eyes regularly and seek professional advice early. Protecting your sight begins before symptoms appear.

item.title: Marine Areas Bill | Certainty beyond tourism
item.description: Businesses make long-term investments based on certainty about the rights they hold, the costs they will face and the rules that will apply throughout the life of a project. The Commercial Use of Marine Areas (CUMA) Bill 2025 proposes a significant change to Fiji’s marine ownership framework.
item.content:encoded:
Businesses make long-term investments based on certainty about the rights they hold, the costs they will face and the rules that will apply throughout the life of a project.

The Commercial Use of Marine Areas (CUMA) Bill 2025 proposes a significant change to Fiji’s marine ownership framework.

It seeks to transfer ownership of certain marine areas used for commercial purposes to customary owners and establish a compensation scheme for their access and use.

These areas may include the water, foreshore, seabed, airspace and certain natural or reclaimed land.

The proposed changes could affect investment confidence, access to finance, operating costs and the long-term viability of tourism businesses.

Their implications may also extend across the wider business ecosystem because tourism operators rely on banks, insurers, investors, contractors, transport providers, suppliers and professional services.

If the new framework creates additional costs or uncertainty for tourism developments, connected businesses could also be affected through delayed projects, reduced spending or changes to existing commercial arrangements.

FCEF supports the fair recognition of customary interests and the principle that communities should benefit appropriately from commercial activity within their traditional areas.

However, a reform of this significance must also provide clarity on existing legal interests, future compensation obligations and the regulatory processes that businesses will be required to follow.

Fair recognition and business certainty should not be treated as competing objectives; a carefully designed framework should deliver both.

In their official submission to the Parliament’s Standing Committee on Justice, Law and Human Rights, the Fiji Hotel and Tourism Association (FHTA) included 14 recommendations that the Government and the Sub-Committee must take into account before passing the bill. These include:

1. Reset the consultation process – Undertake transparent and structured consultation with tourism and marine operators, customary owners throughout Fiji, financial institutions, affected communities, public agencies and other stakeholders before the Bill proceeds.

2. Reconsider the proprietary ownership-transfer model – Determine whether the Bill’s objectives can be achieved through statutory recognition, benefit-sharing, consultation and co-management while preserving State ownership and coherent national regulation of marine areas.

3. Clarify the Bill’s scope and legal effect – Clearly define the rights transferred by a vesting order, the rights and responsibilities retained by the State, the public rights that continue, and the activities, organisations and supporting services captured by the Bill. ‘Commercial tourism activity’ and the practical limits of ‘marine area’ should be settled in the Bill itself, including appropriate exclusions for developed reclaimed land, existing State leases, declared port areas, navigation channels and established public infrastructure.

4. Complete independent economic and fiscal assessments – Assess the likely effects of the Bill on investment, financing, property values, operating costs, employment, consumer prices, State revenue, public infrastructure and Fiji’s competitiveness before enactment. A further project-specific assessment should be required before vesting any area where significant existing or proposed activity may be affected.

5. Establish a clear and nationally consistent compensation framework – Define ‘fair and equitable’ compensation through a transparent methodology, clarify the role of the iTaukei Fisheries Commission, distinguish compensation from rent and other payments, and ensure that compensation remains proportionate and commercially sustainable.

6. Prohibit double compensation and recognise existing arrangements – Credit prior rents, premiums, access payments, conservation contributions, goodwill payments and community benefits against any new liability. Existing compensation and community arrangements should not be reopened without the written agreement of affected parties or an independent legal determination.

7. Automatically preserve existing legal interests – Protect existing leases, licences, concessions, approvals, easements, mortgages, compensation agreements and State-approved projects for their existing terms. These interests should not be compulsorily renegotiated or altered solely because a marine area is vested. The Bill should also provide a staged and managed transition, preserve existing arrangements under the Regulation of Surfing Areas Act, and require consultation on draft regulations and an implementation roadmap before commencement.

8. Strengthen governance, procedural fairness and judicial oversight – Require clear statutory criteria, independent technical and legal advice, conflict-of-interest safeguards, public notice, access to evidence, meaningful objection rights and written reasons for decisions.

The Tribunal must be independent and appropriately qualified, judicial review must remain available, and TLTB must operate under published service standards, decision timeframes, fee schedules and proportionate enforcement procedures.

9. Verify customary ownership and boundaries before vesting – Require independent mapping and surveying, publication of boundaries and supporting evidence, notice to all affected parties, a formal objection process and final resolution of overlapping claims before any vesting order is made. A publicly accessible register of verified owners, boundaries, vested areas and conditions should be maintained.

10. Protect public access, maritime operations and essential State functions – Preserve lawful passage, navigation, anchoring, mooring, recreational and subsistence use, and ordinary access to marine areas. Vesting should not disrupt ports, shipping, inter-island transport, emergency access, public infrastructure, utilities, disaster response, environmental regulation or national security.

11. Preserve State leases, minerals, revenue and infrastructure rights – Clarify responsibility for administering existing State leases and collecting revenue after vesting. State ownership of minerals and the operation, maintenance and future development of ports, channels, jetties, utilities, coastal works and other essential infrastructure must remain protected.

12. Protect and encourage conservation partnerships – Exclude genuine non-commercial conservation, restoration, research and environmental-stewardship activities from inappropriate fees and compensation obligations. Existing marine protected areas, locally managed marine areas and community conservation arrangements should be recognised and preserved.

13. Develop a more balanced alternative framework – Consider a statutory benefit-sharing and co-management model supported, where appropriate, by a nationally administered funding mechanism. Any funding model should be introduced only after consultation and economic assessment and should include transparent collection, distribution, reporting and auditing arrangements.

14. Promote active iTaukei economic participation – Complement compensation and benefit-sharing with enterprise development, access to finance, skills training, joint ventures, equity participation, procurement opportunities and support for iTaukei-owned tourism, conservation, transport and marine-service businesses. Taken together, these measures would provide a more balanced framework for recognising customary interests and delivering fair economic benefits without undermining existing rights, public access, investor confidence, national infrastructure or the coordinated management of Fiji’s marine resources.

The Bill also provides for a compensation scheme between customary owners and affected interest holders. It also states that payments must not be unreasonable or burdensome and should, as far as practicable, be borne by consumers or users of the commercial activity.

The way compensation is determined therefore matters not only to the business making the payment; it may also affect the price paid by visitors and other users.

Many tourism businesses already contribute through access payments, leases, employment, local procurement, community projects, infrastructure and environmental initiatives.

A fair framework should recognise these contributions and guard against overlapping obligations. It should explain, in simple terms, how compensation will be assessed, what existing arrangements will be considered and how disagreements will be resolved. A transparent and consistent national approach would provide greater confidence and fairness for all parties.

item.title: FIJI GETAWAYS | Explore Fiji on a budget
item.description: YOU don’t need to break the bank to tick Fiji off your bucket list. From underwater wonders to foodie and cultural experiences, there are a wealth of activities (pun intended) that can suit a tighter travel budget. Add these things to do in Fiji to your holiday itinerary for an affordable island getaway. Exploring Fiji’s spectacular waterfalls is an ideal way to spend a low-cost travel day. Most w
item.content:encoded:
YOU don’t need to break the bank to tick Fiji off your bucket list. From underwater wonders to foodie and cultural experiences, there are a wealth of activities (pun intended) that can suit a tighter travel budget. Add these things to do in Fiji to your holiday itinerary for an affordable island getaway.

Exploring Fiji’s spectacular waterfalls is an ideal way to spend a low-cost travel day. Most waterfalls are community-run and require a small entry fee. Check with your resort if they run regular waterfall tours otherwise the local bus and taxis are an affordable option if you’re splitting the ride between a few people. If you plan ahead, you should also pack a picnic lunch with snacks from a nearby supermarket (just be sure to take all rubbish back out with you). Consult this guide to Fiji’s best waterfalls for more information on a swimming hole near your resort.

Fiji’s colourful community markets are an absolute must-do for any budget travel itinerary if the timing aligns with your trip. Suva’s ROC Market comes to life on the 3rd Sunday of every month and the Vuda Beach Market at the First Landing Resort near Nadi is held on the second Saturday each month. Both markets showcase a diverse array of local vendors selling hand made goods, delicious street food, fresh produce and more. Whether you want to window shop or treat yourself to some thing small to take home, these markets are an enjoyable way to spend a few hours.

Heritage sites and National Parks are an inexpensive excursion that’ll introduce you to Fiji beyond the beautiful beaches. The Fiji Museum in Suva is a treasure trove of the nation’s past, offering low-cost admission and an impressive collection of archaeological artefacts. Alternatively, take a trip back in time with a visit to the best historical sites in Levuka, Fiji’s first capital and only UNESCO World Heritage site. And, if you’re staying along the Coral Coast, the Sigatoka Sand Dunes are well worth a visit for their natural beauty and ancient settlements, while the Momi Bay Historical Park offers history buffs an in sight into Fiji’s WWII history.

Hiking is one of the best activities for travelers trying to keep costs down. Many island resorts have a favourite (and free) peak hike nearby where their guests can go for the best sunrise and sunset pics. Otherwise, popular walks like the Colo-I Suva Forest Park or Lavena Coastal Walk have a small entry fee that covers the up keep of the trails and facilities and/or goes to the nearby villages, and you can sometimes pay a bit more for a local guide. Find out more about Fiji’s best walks and hikes in this helpful guide.

Water babies will love the many mind blowing snorkeling spots scattered throughout Fiji’s islands. You can snorkel right off the beach in regions like the Coral Coast on Viti Levu, Mamanuca and Yasawa islands or take a short boat ride to the rich, colourful outer reefs in other regions. Bring your own snorkeling gear from home to keep costs down or rent some from your hotel and spend your time discovering the vibrant marine life that lives just below the surface.

Do you know your soursop from your breadfruit? Introduce your palate to fresh tropical delights at a local produce market, the best ones are on Saturdays where you’ll find loads of variety and a buzzing atmosphere. And fruit isn’t the only thing on offer, you can also find unusual local foods like root crops, local spices and substantial cooked seafood packs full of fresh ocean to-market delicacies.

Consider yourself a foodie? There’s a whole world of Fijian cuisine to dive into if you know where to go. The urban areas of Suva, Nadi, Lautoka, Labasa, Savusavu and Sigatoka boast a melting pot of restaurants serving up dishes influenced by indigenous Fijian, Indian, Chinese and European flavours. One of the delights of eating at local restaurants is the affordability, you can get a hearty meal from as little as $10-20FJD, and even at fancier restaurants you’ll pay reasonable prices compared to tourist-heavy areas or resorts.

Pampering yourself is possible too if you unwind at the geothermal mud pools in Sabeto near Nadi. The Sabeto and Tifajek mud pools are usually included in Nadi sightseeing tours if you want to tack on other activities like the Garden of the Sleeping Giant or a village tour too, otherwise you can easily reach them by local bus or taxi.

From sporting competitions to music festivals and cultural exhibits, Fiji’s got loads going on! Catch a rugby game, get amongst vibrant street parades or attend a local art show. Many local events offer entertainment for no or low cost. Check if your trip coincides with any big events on the Tourism Fiji website.

You can sunbathe on the golden sands of Fiji’s beaches without spending a cent. Most coastal resorts have their own beach access, but you’ll also find popular public beaches in Pacific Harbour and the Coral Coast. Keep costs low by bringing your own snorkeling gear, reef-safe sunblock from home, and some snacks for a DIY picnic lunch.

The colourful Sri Siva Subramaniya Temple in Nadi town is another must do. For a small entry fee, you can admire the intricate carvings, vivid colours and the monumental gopuram (entrance tower) on a self-guided tour or spend a bit more to get a local guide and learn about how Indian heritage has influenced modern-day Fiji. After the temple visit be sure to pop into Saravana Bhavan next door, a top-rated vegetarian restaurant serving up dosas, curries and vadas. Yum!

Whether you’re travelling with kiddos or just love some good ‘ole competition, minigolf is always great value and fun. Nestled luxury between the Denarau Golf & Racquet Club, and the Big Bula Waterpark, the Denarau Golf Centre & Mini Golf has an 18 hole course fit for all ages. Grab your club and pair up in a family group or channel your inner Tiger Woods and challenge your friends to a little playtime. Open daily.

Experience Fiji’s beauty with a leisurely horseback ride along the beach. The best places to go horseback riding in Fiji are all Viti Levu and run by small community-based operators. Natadola is your go to spot for beautiful beach views while Wailoaloa Beach in Nadi boasts amazing sunsets. And at Biausevu village on the Coral Coast, you can opt to ride a horse to the waterfall instead of walking the track. Affordable and memorable, these rustic horse rides are an excellent way to soak in Fiji’s coastal charm.

Soak up the sun, sea and a healthy dose of exercise when you explore the ocean and waterways by kayak or stand-up paddleboard. Most coastal resorts offer these non- motorised water sports as a complimentary activity for their guests. The joy of exploration and the soothing, rhythmic paddling will also work wonders for your mental well-being. Plan these activities in the morning, before the wind, sun and waves pick up.

item.title: POINT OF ORIGIN I Castaway Island Resort
item.description: ON July 6, 2026, Castaway Island Resort celebrated its 60th anniversary marking a significant milestone for the Mamanuca based retreat. Located on Qalito Island and facing the vast oceanic expanse of crystal blue waters, Castaway Island Resort has grown and established itself as one of Fiji’s beloved family resorts.
item.content:encoded:
ON July 6, 2026, Castaway Island Resort celebrated its 60th anniversary marking a significant milestone for the Mamanuca based retreat.

Located on Qalito Island and facing the vast oceanic expanse of crystal blue waters, Castaway Island Resort has grown and established itself as one of Fiji’s beloved family resorts.

Today, the resort covers about 17 acres of the private island and features a wide variety of facilities that has kept countless guests entertained over the past six decades.

So, for the uninitiated, it would come as a surprise that Castaway Island Resort’s origins started on July 6, 1966, with a single thatched bure.

The resort gained notoriety and momentum when it was bought by the late Geoff Shaw who later became an influential figure in Fiji’s tourism industry.

His footprints and influence spanned between the shores of the Mamanucas, Nadi and the Coral Coast.

In one of his last interviews with this masthead, Mr Shaw recalled his association with Castaway which began in the early 1990s when the resort was 26 years old.

“It was in 1992 and of course Castaway was in receivership that time so I thought there was an opportunity to see if I could purchase a property that was iconic in the Mamanuca region,” he said.

“My accountant thought I was crazy and he said how are you going to do this, you don’t have any money, but I had another little property in those days called the Reef Hotel.

“I had this idea back in those days that I wanted to, in fact, recreate what the Reef was and build it into what is today the Outrigger.”

Mr Shaw bought Castaway when it went into receivership and had a dream to convert the property into a family focused island getaway.

He had said the success of each project he undertook relied heavily on its people.

“It’s not just our product – our people make the product and with their support and dedication, taking ownership of what my vision was at that time.

Under the late Mr Shaw’s stewardship, Castaway Island became synonymous with authentic, barefoot island hospitality, a blueprint that drew guests back year after year and established the resort as one of the defining properties in Pacific tourism.

That legacy endures in the resort’s hosts, some of whom have worked on the island for more than 30 years, and in the guests who have made Castaway Island Resort a family tradition across generations.

In 2014, Castaway Island changed ownership after Mr Shaw sold the property to Outrigger Enterprises Group.

Castaway Enterprise Group was then acquired by Denver-based KSL Capital Partners LLC.

Under the present owners, the resort has grown into one of the Mamanuca island group’s most popular retreats amassing accolades at the Fiji Tourism Excellence Awards over the past two decades and a front runner in conservation efforts through the Mamanuca Environment Society and the Outrigger Resorts and Hotels led initiative Outrigger Zone.

According to the resort, the program allows the resort to focus on integrating the island’s ecosystem with the guest experience.

In 2025 alone, the resort launched a Sculptural Coral Gene Bank in partnership with non-profit Counting Coral which is a marine-grade steel installation housing more than 500 carefully selected parent corals and is designed to support the long-term regeneration of the surrounding reef.

The resort also collaborated in the translocation of 15 endangered Fijian Crested Iguanas to Qalito Island marking their return after more than 40 years.

Last year, Castaway became the second property in Fiji to earn the Green Key Certification signifying its commitment to sustainability and serving as an assurance for guests that it adheres to strict environmental requirements.

Resort general manager Steven Andrews said the resort offered a rare hospitality experience that’s more than a destination.

“It has allowed travellers to connect with each other and for generations of families to bond across six decades,” Mr Andrew said.

“The loyalty of our guests and the dedication of our hosts are a testament to what happens when a destination is built on authenticity.

“It’s the reason why our returnees and multigenerational families continue to call Castaway Island ‘home’.

“We’re proud to steward this legacy and are excited for everything the next decade holds as we invite more travellers to discover our island home for the first time.”

Later this year, the resort will kick start a week-long celebration themed around 1960s vintage and a nod to the era in which it was born.

A resort statement explained the program will include a traditional Fijian welcome ceremony, a Returnee Guest Appreciation Day, a Management Cocktail Evening, an Environment Day centred on coral planting and the Coral Gene Bank, and a Cocktail Gala on November 27.

Until then the resort introduced a guest and host driven storytelling campaign, inviting generations of loyal guests to share their favourite memories through photos, videos and personal reflections. The campaign will also spotlight longtime hosts whose stories have helped shape the resort’s enduring Bula spirit of hospitality.

item.title: BACK IN HISTORY I Significant milestone – Rewa Dairy opens UHT milk processing, packaging plant
item.description: Fiji’s dairy industry once stood at the heart of the nation’s drive toward self-sufficiency. One of its defining moments came with the official opening of the Rewa Co-operative Dairy Company’s Ultra Heat Treatment (UHT) milk processing and packaging plant, which marked a major step forward for local milk production.
item.content:encoded:
Fiji’s dairy industry once stood at the heart of the nation’s drive toward self-sufficiency.

One of its defining moments came with the official opening of the Rewa Co-operative Dairy Company’s Ultra Heat Treatment (UHT) milk processing and packaging plant, which marked a major step forward for local milk production.

According to a The Fiji Times article published on March 9, 1988, the inauguration was officiated by the then Minister for Primary Industries, Villame Gonelevu, who described the dairy industry as an essential pillar of Fiji’s economy and nutrition.

“The dairy industry is important to Fiji for its well-known product, milk, which is often called a complete food and consumed by all in one form or another,” Mr Gonelevu said.

At the time, Fiji was focused on reducing its dependence on imported dairy products while creating greater opportunities for local farmers.

The industry supplied milk and cream through about 200 registered dairy farms, with more than 75 per cent supplying Rewa Dairy.

The company collected almost 20,000 litres of milk and 10,000 kilograms of cream each day, producing a range of products including pasteurised milk, flavoured milk, butter, cheese, cultured dairy products and powdered milk.

The new Ultra Heat Treatment (UHT) plant enabled Rewa Dairy to package milk in long-life cartons that could be stored for up to six months without refrigeration before opening, making fresh-quality milk more accessible to rural communities and the outer islands.

Speaking at the opening ceremony, Mr Gonelevu emphasised the industry’s key objectives, which included increasing local milk production to improve national self-sufficiency, strengthening rural incomes, creating employment on dairy farms and in processing facilities, and improving the nutritional wellbeing of Fiji’s population.

The minister also praised Rewa Dairy for exceeding its projected milk production target despite the severe drought, describing the achievement as evidence of the industry’s resilience and promising future.

The launch of the UHT facility also had an immediate social impact.

During the ceremony, the minister unveiled a 900-litre gift pack of Rewa Life milk, which was distributed to families in need, symbolising the company’s commitment to supporting local communities.

For a long time, Rewa Dairy remained one of Fiji’s best-known food manufacturers, and the opening of its UHT processing plant stood as one of the company’s most significant milestones in the development of Fiji’s dairy industry.

The investment demonstrated how innovation, government support and the commitment of local farmers could work together to strengthen food security and reduce Fiji’s reliance on imported dairy products.

More than the opening of a new processing facility, the inauguration of the Ultra Heat Treatment (UHT) milk processing and packaging plant marked an important chapter in Fiji’s agricultural history and laid the foundation for a stronger and more resilient local dairy industry.

item.title: LOOK BACK I Thousands at funeral of family killed in crash
item.description: More than 4500 people crowded Wailoaloa Crematorium in Nadi to pay their last respects to a Nadi family of five killed in a road crash. The article was published in this newspaper on Thursday August 9, 1984.
item.content:encoded:
More than 4500 people crowded Wailoaloa Crematorium in Nadi to pay their last respects to a Nadi family of five killed in a road crash.

The article was published in this newspaper on Thursday August 9, 1984.

Several thousand earlier went to the family’s home at Nawaka where the bodies were placed in five separate coffins.

Relatives and friends wept openly as the coffins were put on a carrier which took them to the cemetery.

Killed in the crash at Semo, Sigatoka were Manik Raj, his wife Nirmal Wati, their son Manoj Kumar and daughters Vimal Kumari and Saroj Kumari.

They were driving back from Sigatoka after visiting relatives when their car collided with a Fiji Gas van coming from the opposite side.

Mr Raj was a maintenance foreman at Westgate Hotel while Manoj attended Shri Vivekananda High School, and his sisters attended Andrews Primary School in Nadi.

Teachers and students from the schools and hotel staff were among mourners at the funeral.

At the Wailoaloa crematorium, the bodies were taken out of the coffins and placed on a single pyre on the seashore.

Before the bodies were cremated people filed past to pay their last respects to the family.

Mr Raj left behind his mother and two sisters while Wati is survived by two brothers and four sisters.

Raj and Wati had been married for twenty years.

item.title: TRAVEL I Korovou’s best kept secret is back on the menu
item.description: THERE is no need for mad rush in the laid-back township of Korovou. Here the clock seems to tik tok a little slower, reminding keen travellers that some of Fiji’s unforgettable experiences are found tucked away from the city’s hurried pace.
item.content:encoded:
THERE is no need for mad rush in the laid-back township of Korovou.

Here the clock seems to tik tok a little slower, reminding keen travellers that some of Fiji’s unforgettable experiences are found tucked away from the city’s hurried pace.

Drive into the heart of Tailevu North and, perched above the township with sweeping views of the lush countryside, sits the newly renovated Tailevu Hotel, a familiar landmark that is rewriting a new chapter.

For years, the hotel has been a resting place for weary travellers, government workers and families passing through the district.

Today, it is giving people another reason to stop, not just for the night, but for a memorable meal.

Step inside and the first thing you notice is the warmth.

There is no pretence in the air – just genuine Fijian hospitality from a small team that welcomes guests with easy smiles and attentive service.

Then comes the food. The new breakfast, lunch and dinner menu is a celebration of Tailevu itself, fresh, generous and proudly local. Every plate reflects the abundance of the province, where organic vegetables grow in nearby farms, fish arrive fresh from the coast and traditional recipes continue to be passed from one generation to the next.

Behind the menu is chef Asupa Leba, who believes good food should be accessible to everyone.

Before taking charge of the kitchen in Korovou, the Totoya, Lau islander honed her skills at the Shangri-La Fijian Resort on the Coral Coast before moving on to some of Suva’s well-known cafés and coffee houses.

Those experiences shaped her appreciation for quality dining, but it was Korovou that perhaps inspired her latest creation.

“I walked around town to see what people were eating,” she said.

“I realised there wasn’t a place where families could enjoy affordable fine dining in a beautiful setting. That’s what inspired this menu.”

It is a philosophy that is reflected in every dish. Breakfast begins with a generous big breakfast – crispy toast, fluffy omelette, sausages and perfectly cooked bacon, of course with your favoursite choice of juice or hot beverage.

It is simple, hearty and satisfying, with plans already underway to introduce more traditional Fijian breakfast favourites.

By lunchtime, the kitchen is in full swing. One dish, in particular, tells the story of Tailevu better than words ever could.

For just $18, the catch-of-the-day platter brings together crispy fried fish, stuffed freshwater mussels, creamy kokoda, fresh miti ota, comforting rourou balls with a tuna filling and golden eggplant fritters.

Every bite is a reminder that Fiji’s finest ingredients often come from its own backyard.

As the afternoon sun softens over Korovou and the hills begin to glow, dinner offers another taste of home.

A steaming bowl of tender sui served alongside fresh rourou or moca is comfort food at its best—rich, wholesome and deeply rooted in local tradition. Alternatively, you might like to sink into fish cooked in rich coconut cream.

But the experience doesn’t end at the dining table.

Enjoy a refreshing drink at the nearby bar before heading into the hotel’s dance hall, where locals and visitors alike gather as familiar island tunes fill the air.

It’s the kind of place where strangers quickly become friends, and where an evening can effortlessly stretch into a night of laughter, music and dancing.

In many ways, the Tailevu Hotel mirrors the township around it. It is unassuming with its attractions and full of surprises too. For travellers making their way along Kings Road, the hotel is more than a convenient stopover.

It is a chance to slow down, enjoy honest food prepared by Ms Leba and her team, and experience the warmth of a community that has always known how to make visitors feel at home.

Sometimes the best journeys are not about racing to the next destination but a warm welcome, a beautifully prepared meal and a place that reminds you why you chose to travel in the first place.

That place is Korovou, where the Tailevu Hotel is ready to embrace you, breakfast, lunch and dinner!!
